# Skills and Automations
URL: https://atlas.aziro.com/docs/skills/

# Skills and automations

A skill is a runbook: the steps someone repeats to do a job — triage a timeout,
restart a deployment, check a release — written down once, reviewed, and
handed to every connected assistant to follow. Atlas can mine skills from the
procedures it watches people repeat, or you can write one by hand; either way a
skill moves through review before any agent sees it. Reach for this when your
team keeps solving the same problem the same way.

## Open It

The **AUTOMATE** group in the dashboard rail holds three views:

- **Skill Studio** (`#/studio`) — review what the miner found, edit a skill and
  preview the `SKILL.md` an agent will read.
- **Skills** (`#/automations`) — the registry: every stored version and where it
  is in its lifecycle.
- **Approvals** (`#/approvals`, titled **Action Queue**) — everything waiting
  for a human decision: skills submitted for trust, the actions Atlas derived
  from incidents, and requests from the graph.

From the terminal the same work is `atlas skill` (author, test, render,
distribute) and `atlas recall` (mine frequent prompts, move automations
through their lifecycle, sync with an org Atlas).

![Skill Studio with no mined trajectories, its filters for automatability and side-effect tier, and one registered candidate skill](assets/docs/skills/skill-studio.png "Skill Studio on the demo service: episode capture is off, so nothing is mined yet; one skill was registered by hand.")

## Follow a Skill Through Its Lifecycle

Every skill version is in one of five states. The **Skill lifecycle** strip on
the Skills page counts them; click a stage to filter the registry.

| State | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **candidate** | registered, not yet reviewed |
| **validating** | submitted for trust; waiting in the Action Queue |
| **trusted** | advertised to connected agents; runbooks are rendered as `SKILL.md` files |
| **quarantined** | pulled from agents pending review |
| **revoked** | permanently withdrawn |

![The Skills page: lifecycle strip with one candidate, the registry list, and the selected skill's runbook steps, rendered SKILL.md and contract](assets/docs/skills/skills-registry.png "A candidate runbook in the registry: its steps with their side-effect tiers, the rendered SKILL.md, and its contract.")

Selecting a skill shows its **Runbook steps**, each tagged with a side-effect
tier (`read`, `mutate-local`, `mutate-shared`, `destructive`, `credential` or
`unknown`), the **Rendered SKILL.md**, and its **Contract**: params,
preconditions, verify, rollback and the files whose change makes it stale.
Versions are immutable — a change is a new version that goes through review
again.

The Command Center shows the same counts in its **Skills lifecycle** panel:

![The Command Center's Skills lifecycle panel: candidate 0, validating 0, trusted 1, quarantined 0, revoked 0](assets/docs/skills/skills-lifecycle-panel.png "Skills lifecycle on the Command Center, read from the recall registry.")

## Let Atlas Find Repeated Work

Mining needs episodes: the sessions your assistants run, captured with prompts
redacted. A service does not read your agents' transcripts unless you opt in,
and says so when it starts:

```text
episode capture: off — set ATLAS_SERVE_CAPTURE=1 to opt in
```

Turn it on for a service that runs on your own machine:

```sh
ATLAS_SERVE_CAPTURE=1 atlas serve
```

- The service then scans `~/.claude/projects` and `~/.codex/sessions` every
  `ATLAS_SERVE_CAPTURE_SEC` seconds (default 20) into its observability store —
  `telemetry.db` beside the graph, never the graph itself.
- `ATLAS_SERVE_CAPTURE_PROMPT_MODE` decides how prompts are kept: `off` stores
  only a hash, `norm` (the default) stores redacted normalized text, `raw`
  stores redacted prompt text. Tool traces are always redacted.
- `atlas privacy purge-recall --apply --yes` deletes what was captured. See
  [Privacy](privacy).

For a team, `atlas connect` installs the Claude and Codex capture hooks on each
machine instead (see [One Atlas for a team](teams)). Once episodes arrive,
repeated command sequences show up as **Mined trajectories** in Skill Studio —
filter them by **Ready to automate**, kind and tier, sort by **hot**, **ROI**,
**frequency** or **newest** — and on the Command Center under **Ready to
automate**. On the demo service capture is off, so both are empty:

![The Command Center's Ready to automate panel: No procedural clusters mined yet](assets/docs/skills/ready-to-automate.png "Ready to automate stays empty until episodes are captured.")

Recall also mines the questions people ask. Asking the same thing twice is
enough to form a cluster:

```text
$ atlas recall clusters
{"clusters":[{"id":"39da6790b3d067bc","prompt_norm":"what calls modeldenied","frequency":2,"user_count":1,
  "avg_tokens":8822,"hot_score":9691.899128981016,"success_ratio":1,"automatable":"yes","status":"open",…},
 {"id":"5a9649f09806db7b","prompt_norm":"how are allowed models enforced","frequency":2,"user_count":1,
  "avg_tokens":7806,"hot_score":8575.767427903642,"success_ratio":1,"automatable":"yes","status":"open",…}],
 "events":4}
```

`atlas recall promote <id>` distills a cluster into a candidate automation;
`atlas skill new <slug> --from-cluster <id>` prefills a runbook from a mined
trajectory; `atlas skill suggest` ranks clusters by how automatable they are.

## Write a Skill

A skill pack is a folder, `~/.atlas/skills/<slug>/`, holding `skill.yaml`.
Scaffold one, fill it in, then lint and test it:

```text
$ atlas skill new upstream-timeout-triage
scaffolded ~/.atlas/skills/upstream-timeout-triage
edit skill.yaml, then: atlas skill lint upstream-timeout-triage && atlas skill test upstream-timeout-triage
```

```yaml
slug: upstream-timeout-triage
title: Triage upstream provider timeouts in inference-gateway
version: 1
kind: runbook
triggers:
  - groq is timing out
  - failed to generate tokens
  - upstream provider errors on the gateway
params:
  - name: namespace
    default: inference
  - name: deployment
    default: inference-gateway
preconditions:
  - command -v git
steps:
  - run: git log --oneline -5 -- api/routes.go providers/core/provider.go
    expect: the last changes to the chat handler and the provider client
    tier: read
  - run: grep -n "request timed out" api/routes.go
    expect: the call sites that log the timeout
    tier: read
  - run: grep -n "READ_TIMEOUT\|WRITE_TIMEOUT" config/config.go
    expect: the server timeouts the gateway runs with
    tier: read
  - run: kubectl rollout restart deployment/{deployment} -n {namespace}
    expect: a fresh rollout once the provider recovers
    tier: mutate-shared
verify: the error templates for api/routes.go stop growing in Log Streams
rollback: kubectl rollout undo deployment/{deployment} -n {namespace}
staleness:
  ttl_days: 90
  files:
    - api/routes.go
    - providers/core/provider.go
```

`atlas skill test` runs the preflight checks and the `read` steps only, and
prints mutating steps without running them. A step tagged `read` whose command
Atlas cannot prove read-only is refused, not run.

```text
$ atlas skill lint upstream-timeout-triage
ok

$ atlas skill test upstream-timeout-triage
preflight 1: command -v git
/usr/bin/git
  ✓ ok
step 1 (read): git log --oneline -5 -- api/routes.go providers/core/provider.go
0c89a51 feat(telemetry): name outbound spans with method and path (#554)
3199ad2 refactor: gate image stripping on per-model modalities (#549)
…
  ✓ ok
step 2 (read): grep -n "request timed out" api/routes.go
486:  router.logger.Error("request timed out", err, "provider", provider.GetName())
801:  router.logger.Error("request timed out", err, "provider", providerID)
…
  ✓ ok
step 3 (read): grep -n "READ_TIMEOUT\|WRITE_TIMEOUT" config/config.go
96:  ReadTimeout        time.Duration `env:"READ_TIMEOUT, default=30s" description:"Read timeout"`
97:  WriteTimeout       time.Duration `env:"WRITE_TIMEOUT, default=30s" description:"Write timeout"`
  ✓ ok
step 4 (mutate-shared, NOT executed): kubectl rollout restart deployment/inference-gateway -n inference
preflight + read steps pass; mutating steps printed only

$ atlas skill register upstream-timeout-triage
registered upstream-timeout-triage v1 (candidate, kind runbook)
```

Open the registered skill in **Skill Studio** to see it the way a reviewer
will: identity and triggers, params, preconditions, steps with their tiers, and
a live preview of the rendered runbook. A registered version is read-only —
**Fork v2 to edit** starts the next version. **+ New blank skill** starts one
from scratch in the browser.

![Skill Studio showing the registered upstream-timeout-triage runbook: identity, triggers, params, preconditions and the rendered SKILL.md preview](assets/docs/skills/skill-studio-editor.png "The registered runbook in Skill Studio, with the rendered SKILL.md on the right.")

## Review and Trust a Skill

1. In **Skills**, select the candidate and click **Submit for trust**. Its
   state becomes **validating**.
2. Open **Approvals**. The skill waits under **Skill candidates for org trust**
   with its provenance, the first steps and a **HIGH-TIER STEPS** warning for
   anything beyond `read`. **Runbook** opens the full rendered text.
3. Click **Approve as trusted**, or **Quarantine** to send it back.

![Submitting the v2 candidate for trust in Skills, then opening Approvals where it waits under Skill candidates for org trust](assets/docs/skills/submit-for-trust.mp4 "Submit for trust, then review in the Action Queue.")

![The skill trust review card: validating, mutate-shared, provenance, the first three read steps, the high-tier kubectl step and the Approve as trusted button](assets/docs/skills/skill-trust-review.png "The review card shows the one step that changes something shared before you approve.")

**Where trusted skills are written.** Trusting a runbook renders it as
`SKILL.md` files for the agents on the machine that runs the service, under
that process's home directory. On a shared service, set `ATLAS_SKILLS_HOME` to
the directory those files should go to.

The same steps from the terminal, rendering into your own assistants' skill
folders:

```text
$ atlas recall state upstream-timeout-triage trusted
{
  "slug": "upstream-timeout-triage",
  "state": "trusted"
}

$ atlas skill render upstream-timeout-triage --agent claude
rendered upstream-timeout-triage v1 → ~/.claude/skills/atlas-upstream-timeout-triage/SKILL.md
1 skill file(s) written
```

The rendered file opens with the procedure's guard rails — run the preflight
first, stop on any failed step, report the outcome — then the parameters,
preflight and steps.

## Decide What Waits in the Action Queue

**Approvals** is the one place where a person says yes or no. Besides skills it
holds the actions Atlas derived from active incidents — a ticket draft, a pull
request naming the cited files, an alert rule — and requests Atlas raises from
missing route, coverage and freshness signals in the graph.

![The Action Queue: 17 awaiting review, an incident's ticket draft with its rationale, descriptor and blast radius, and the Approve and Reject buttons](assets/docs/skills/action-queue.png "Incident actions in the Action Queue. Each card states what its executor would do; Atlas executes nothing.")

- Each card shows its rationale, what the descriptor asks for, and the blast
  radius if someone runs it.
- **Approve** records the decision and the exact descriptor (by digest) for
  whoever carries it out; **Reject** records the refusal. Decisions are stored
  on the service and listed under **Recent approval activity**.
- Incident actions are also listed, and can be decided, on the incident itself
  — see [Observe](observe).

## From the CLI

```text
$ atlas skill list
{"skills":[{"slug":"upstream-timeout-triage","version":1,"kind":"runbook","state":"candidate",
  "title":"Triage upstream provider timeouts in inference-gateway"}]}

$ atlas recall automations
{"automations":[{"slug":"upstream-timeout-triage","version":1,"kind":"runbook","state":"candidate",
  "prompt_norm":"groq is timing out | failed to generate tokens | upstream provider errors on the gateway",…}],
 "runs":0,"test_runs":0,"tokens_saved_estimated":0,"tokens_saved_measured":0,"tokens_saved_total":0}
```

| Command | Does |
| --- | --- |
| `atlas skill new <slug> [--from-cluster <id>]` | Scaffold a pack, optionally prefilled from a mined trajectory. |
| `atlas skill lint` / `test` | Validate the pack; run preflight and read steps only. |
| `atlas skill register [--trust]` | Publish the pack into the local registry as a candidate. |
| `atlas skill render [slug…] --agent <agent>` | Write trusted runbooks as `SKILL.md` files for `claude`, `codex`, `copilot` or `all`. |
| `atlas skill push` / `pull` / `fork` | Send a skill to the org Atlas (it arrives as an org candidate), fetch org-trusted skills, or fork a read-only org skill into an editable pack. |
| `atlas skill suggest` / `graduations` / `nominate` | Rank automatable clusters; list trusted runbooks that earned a script promotion; push one finished session straight to review. |
| `atlas recall clusters` / `promote` | Mine frequent prompts; distill one into a candidate automation. |
| `atlas recall state <slug> <state>` | Move an automation through candidate, validating, trusted, revoked. |
| `atlas recall push` / `pull` | Sync trusted automations and anonymized cluster stats with the org Atlas. |

See the [CLI reference](cli) for every flag.

## From the API

- `GET /api/v1/skills` — the registered packs the review queue reads.
- `POST /api/v1/recall/automations/{slug}/state` — `{"state": "validating", "version": 2}`
  moves a version through its lifecycle.
- `GET /api/v1/recall/metrics?by=skill` — per-skill savings from the runs
  ledger (recorded replays and script runs).
- `POST /api/v1/dashboard/approvals/{id}` — decide a card in the Action Queue.

State changes and decisions need the read-write token when the service enforces
one. See [Dashboard and HTTP API](service).

## Related

- [Observe](observe) — incidents and the actions they propose.
- [One Atlas for a team](teams) — connect machines so skills sync both ways.
- [AI assistant setup](assistants) — where rendered skills are read by Claude,
  Codex and Copilot.
- [Privacy](privacy) — what episode capture stores and how to purge it.

# AI Assistant Setup
URL: https://atlas.aziro.com/docs/assistants/

# AI Assistant Setup

Atlas registers its MCP server with Claude CLI, Claude Desktop, Codex, Cursor,
Gemini, and GitHub Copilot, so any of these assistants can query your local
code graph. This page covers automatic setup, repository-pinned setup, git
hooks, verification, and removal. For what the tools return once connected,
see [MCP Tools](mcp).

## Automatic Setup with Bootstrap

Use bootstrap when you want every detected assistant provisioned in one pass.
In managed environments, always preview first:

```sh
atlas bootstrap --dry-run
```

The preview names every file bootstrap would write and the entry it would put
there. On a machine with no assistant configured yet it reads (binary path
shortened):

```text
would write ~/.claude.json
  mcpServers.atlas = {command: "/path/to/atlas", args: ["mcp", "--supervise", "--watch=false"]}
would write ~/.claude/skills/atlas/SKILL.md
  skill atlas (claude)
would write ~/.claude/skills/atlas-sre-triage/SKILL.md
  skill atlas-sre-triage (claude)
would write ~/Library/Application Support/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json
  mcpServers.atlas = {command: "/path/to/atlas", args: ["mcp", "--supervise", "--watch=false"]}
would write ~/.cursor/mcp.json
  mcpServers.atlas = {command: "/path/to/atlas", args: ["mcp", "--supervise", "--watch=false"]}
would write ~/.gemini/settings.json
  mcpServers.atlas = {command: "/path/to/atlas", args: ["mcp", "--supervise", "--watch=false"]}
would write ~/.codex/config.toml
  mcp_servers.atlas = {command: "/path/to/atlas", args: ["mcp", "--supervise", "--watch=false"]}
would write ~/.codex/skills/atlas/SKILL.md
  skill atlas (codex)
would write ~/.codex/skills/atlas-sre-triage/SKILL.md
  skill atlas-sre-triage (codex)
would write ~/Library/Application Support/Code/User/mcp.json
  servers.atlas = {command: "/path/to/atlas", args: ["mcp", "--supervise", "--watch=false"]}
would write ~/.copilot/skills/atlas-sre-triage/SKILL.md
  skill atlas-sre-triage (copilot)
```

Besides the `atlas` skill, bootstrap installs `atlas-sre-triage`, the runbook
Atlas ships for answering production questions from the [Observe](observe)
tools. When a client already has an atlas entry, the preview shows the merged
entry, keeping any `--db` or `--repo` you pinned.

Apply the changes:

```sh
atlas bootstrap
```

Restrict provisioning to selected clients, or exclude some:

```sh
atlas bootstrap --only codex,claude,claude-desktop
atlas bootstrap --skip cursor
```

Restart each assistant after its MCP configuration changes; most clients read
MCP configuration only at startup.

### What Bootstrap Writes

Bootstrap registers Atlas as an MCP server and installs the atlas-first skill
plus a CLAUDE.md directive for all detected assistants. It bakes the absolute
binary path into each config and registers the supervised gateway with no
`--db`, so the workspace is resolved at query time rather than pinned at
install time. The command merges the existing atlas entry rather than replacing it, so a `--db` pin, extra args, or an `env` block you configured are preserved. It is idempotent: safe to run repeatedly and from
a package post-install hook. Use `--home` to override the home directory base
when provisioning a different account's configuration.

## Repository-Pinned Setup

Use a repository-pinned local MCP configuration when one assistant should
always query one index:

```sh
cd /path/to/repository
atlas index .

atlas install skill \
  --agent codex,claude,claude-desktop \
  --repo "$PWD" \
  --db "sqlite://$PWD/.atlas/atlas.db" \
  --server-url=none
```

## Dynamic Workspace Setup

Bootstrap is appropriate when the assistant supplies the active workspace at
runtime. Repository-scoped MCP tools still require one of:

- a workspace root supplied by the client
- a `workspace` argument
- a repository ID
- a repository pinned when MCP starts

If none is available, Atlas returns `workspace_required` instead of selecting
a repository silently.

## Shared Local Server

Use one local service when multiple thin clients should share a single index
and watcher:

```sh
atlas serve --mcp

atlas install skill \
  --agent codex,claude,claude-desktop \
  --repo "$PWD" \
  --server-url http://127.0.0.1:3099
```

Use a token before exposing the service beyond loopback. See
[Dashboard and HTTP API](service).

## Keep the Graph Fresh with a Git Hook

Install a local git hook when you want the index updated as part of your
normal git workflow rather than by a running watcher:

```sh
atlas install hook
```

The hook keeps the Atlas graph fresh in the repository where it is installed.

## Client Configuration Locations

Check these paths when auditing what setup wrote or when a client does not
pick up the server:

| Client | Typical location |
| --- | --- |
| Codex | `~/.codex/config.toml` |
| Claude CLI | `~/.claude.json` |
| Claude Desktop on macOS | `~/Library/Application Support/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json` |

Atlas preserves unrelated client configuration. Always review a dry run before
applying changes in managed environments.

## Ask in the Dashboard

The same providers answer in the dashboard's **Ask Workbench**: a conversation
about the codebase where Atlas gathers the evidence and the model writes the
cited answer. A `claude` or `codex` CLI that is installed and logged in is
detected automatically; an API key can be stored with `atlas llm set`. Check
what is configured with:

```sh
atlas llm status
atlas llm detect --apply
```

In the dashboard the same configuration is under **System › App integrations
› AI providers** (`#/system?tab=integrations`): each provider's state
(**default**, **detected**, **ready**), its model and credential, a **Test**
button, and **Detect** to look for installed CLIs again.

![System › App integrations › AI providers: two providers detected and ready, Claude as the default via the anthropic-cli provider, model claude-sonnet-5, credential cli_login](assets/docs/assistants/ai-providers.png "AI providers, detected automatically from the logged-in claude and codex CLIs.")

See [Ask Workbench](workbench) for how a turn works, the threads the server
keeps, and what leaves the machine.

## Verify

Confirm the integration end to end before relying on it:

```sh
atlas doctor --verify atlas
atlas status
atlas bootstrap --dry-run
```

`doctor --verify atlas` also checks for binary drift: whether the `atlas` on
`PATH` — what assistants launch via `command:"atlas"` — matches the running
binary. Then ask the assistant a repository-specific question and confirm that
the answer includes source file and line references.

## Remove the Integration

Preview removal, then apply it:

```sh
atlas uninstall --dry-run
atlas uninstall
```

Uninstall reverses `atlas bootstrap` across every assistant it provisions: it
removes the atlas MCP server entry from each config, the atlas skill markdown,
and the atlas-managed block in the global CLAUDE.md. Nothing else is touched —
other MCP servers, unrelated config keys, and your own CLAUDE.md content
outside the atlas markers are preserved. Re-running reports `absent` and
writes nothing. By default repository indexes are not deleted; `atlas uninstall --purge` also removes the `.atlas` index directories (global `~/.atlas` + every registry repo root), printing the blast radius and total reclaimed first and requiring confirmation (`--yes` to skip, `--dry-run` to preview). See
[Privacy and Data Handling](privacy) for data removal.

---

# MCP Tools
URL: https://atlas.aziro.com/docs/mcp/

# MCP Tools

Atlas exposes its graph, search, and impact analysis as MCP tools, so a
connected assistant answers repository questions with bounded, cited context
instead of raw file dumps. This page covers the transports, the tool set, how
workspace scope is resolved, and how to keep responses small.

## Transports

Choose the transport based on how the client launches Atlas. Desktop agents
spawn a process and speak stdio; shared setups talk HTTP to one long-running
service.

Stdio (the default; local to the launching assistant):

```sh
atlas mcp --transport stdio
```

HTTP, mounted on the local service at `POST /mcp`:

```sh
atlas serve --mcp
```

`atlas mcp` can also serve HTTP directly with `--http 127.0.0.1:8765`
(Streamable HTTP) or `--sse 127.0.0.1:8766` (legacy HTTP+SSE); set
`ATLAS_API_TOKEN` to require `Authorization: Bearer` on either. With
`--supervise`, Atlas runs as the supervised warm MCP gateway: it uses the
workspace database, starts a background watch, and serves `code_query` first.
By default the MCP process also watches the repository to keep the graph
fresh (`--watch=false` or `ATLAS_NO_WATCH=1` to disable; `--watch-path` to
watch a different path).

## Tool Selection

| Tool | Use it for |
| --- | --- |
| `code_query` | Natural-language questions about a repository |
| `search` | Focused lexical or semantic discovery |
| `symbol` | Definitions, snippets, callers, callees, refs, and coverage |
| `graph` | Paths or neighborhoods between symbols |
| `impact` | Repository or cross-repository blast radius |
| `routes` | Served routes, consumers, and dependencies |
| `context` | Code-review context for changed paths |
| `report` | Repository-level code intelligence reports |
| `history` | Indexed history and graph changes |
| `status` | Index, readiness, and retrieval state |
| `link` | Register a repository for workspace or cross-repository analysis |
| `record_feedback` | Record result-quality feedback |
| `record_task` | Record the outcome of a procedural task |

## Choosing a Tool

Start with `code_query` for most repository questions: it checks index
readiness and returns cited context under a bounded response budget. Reach for
a narrower tool when you already know the shape of the answer:

- `symbol` when you have a name and want its definition, callers, callees,
  refs, or coverage. Add package, receiver, or arity filters when the name is
  overloaded. Since 0.1.55 an owner-qualified name — `Type.method`,
  `Widget.prototype.render`, a Go `pkg.Func` — resolves on every view,
  including the default `explain`
  ([#150](https://github.com/aziron-ai/atlas/issues/150)), and `mutations: true` on the refs view lists only the
  references that write a symbol ([#55](https://github.com/aziron-ai/atlas/issues/55)).
- `context` when reviewing a known set of changed files.
- `impact` before a change, to size its blast radius.
- `routes` for service contracts, consumers, and dependencies.
- `report` for whole-graph analytics. Since 0.1.55 its `hubs` and
  `communities` sections are the whole `atlas hubs` / `atlas communities`
  answers — objects carrying `eligible`, `excluded_isolated`, `warnings` and
  the community split, rows capped by `limit` — rather than bare arrays
  ([#45](https://github.com/aziron-ai/atlas/issues/45)).
- `status` when results look empty or stale — it reports index and readiness
  state, which distinguishes "no index" from "no matches". Since 0.1.55 it
  also carries a `telemetry` block, so a read-only server says
  `unavailable_read_only` instead of leaving fields out
  ([#154](https://github.com/aziron-ai/atlas/issues/154)).

## Workspace Scoping

Repository-scoped tools need to know which repository they operate on. Atlas
accepts scope from, in order of availability:

- a workspace root supplied by the client
- a `workspace` argument on the call
- a repository ID
- a repository pinned at launch time with `--repo`

If none is available, Atlas returns `workspace_required` instead of silently
choosing a repository.

**Since 0.1.55**, more of these signals resolve, and a refusal says which one
it judged:

- **Windows roots.** A root a Windows client declares — `file:///C:/…`, VS
  Code's `file:///c%3A/…`, `file://localhost/C:/…`, a UNC path or a plain
  `C:\` path — resolves to its directory and matches without regard to case or
  separators. This is verified by tests on macOS; a run on Windows is still
  pending ([#72](https://github.com/aziron-ai/atlas/issues/72)).
- **Checkouts Atlas did not index.** A `workspace` that is a linked worktree,
  another clone or a worktree of a bare clone of an indexed repository is
  served by that index when its HEAD and working-tree state equal the latest
  snapshot; the scope reason is `workspace_identity`. Several equal checkouts
  are refused as `ambiguous_repo` with `candidates[]` and a remedy to pass
  `repo_id` ([#42](https://github.com/aziron-ai/atlas/issues/42)).
- **Refusals name their source.** A scope refusal carries `scope_source`
  (`workspace`, `cwd`, `roots` or `launch_roots`). A miss on client roots
  alone lists each root it tried in `roots_tried[]` (`path`, `uri`, and what
  is at that path), and a `workspace_not_indexed` refusal names the
  `searched_stores` and a `checkout` diagnosis (`content_differs`,
  `not_a_git_checkout`) beside `repos[]` and `remedy`
  ([#72](https://github.com/aziron-ai/atlas/issues/72),
  [#42](https://github.com/aziron-ai/atlas/issues/42)).

## Result Statuses

Check the status field before trusting a result — it tells you whether the
answer is backed by an index at all.

| Status | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `ok` | Atlas returned cited context |
| `indexing` | An index was started or is still running |
| `no_index` | No usable index exists for the workspace |
| `insufficient` | The index could not support a cited answer — nothing citeable is indexed, or (since 0.1.55, with `require_citations`) the retrieved code does not carry what the question names: `reason: citations_below_relevance_floor` |
| `budget_exceeded` | Strict output budget was too small |
| `workspace_required` | Repository scope was not declared |
| `workspace_not_indexed` | The workspace has no index this server can use; retry `code_query` with `allow_lazy_index=true`, or re-call with one of `repos[]` |
| `ambiguous_repo` | Several repositories match; re-call with one of `candidates[]` as `repo_id` |

## Citations and the Relevance Floor

A non-empty citation list is not evidence on its own: keyword search always
matches something. **Since 0.1.55**, `code_query` with
`require_citations: true` also checks that the cited symbol names and paths
carry what the question names — an identifier it spells, or enough of its
specific terms ([#60](https://github.com/aziron-ai/atlas/issues/60)). Below
that floor it refuses:

| Field | When | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `status` | refused | `insufficient`, with no `citations` and no `context` |
| `reason` | refused | `citations_below_relevance_floor` — stable; branch on it |
| `relevance` | refused, or `ok` with pruned citations | the verdict (`below_floor` or `grounded`), what grounded it, the terms it looked for and matched, and how many citations it pruned |
| `low_confidence_hits` | refused, or `ok` with pruned citations | up to 5 candidates with the words they matched — never citations, never evidence |

On a grounded answer, a keyword-only citation that matched only generic words
moves to `low_confidence_hits`; graph evidence is never pruned. An answer the
floor did not touch is unchanged. Trimming to `max_tokens` never removes the
last citation: a budget that cannot hold one is refused with
`budget_exceeded`, and the message names the budget that would fit
([#160](https://github.com/aziron-ai/atlas/issues/160)).

**Evidence inside large functions.** The index keeps a bounded window of each
body. When a cited symbol is longer than that window, `code_query` and
`context` re-read the lines that match the question from the file — only when
the file still has the indexed hash — and serve the signature, up to 4
windows and the closing line, with each skipped run marked
`// ... elided N lines (La-Lb) ...`. `metadata.body_elision` records what was
shown and elided, or why the file was not used (`source_changed`,
`source_unavailable`, `source_too_large`, `budget_trimmed`, `focus_cap`); the
citation keeps the symbol's real line range
([#156](https://github.com/aziron-ai/atlas/issues/156)).

## Freshness Fields

**Since 0.1.55**, `code_query`, `symbol` (every view), `search` and `context`
answers say how their snapshot relates to the checkout, with the same fields
the CLI and HTTP API return ([#59](https://github.com/aziron-ai/atlas/issues/59),
[#62](https://github.com/aziron-ai/atlas/issues/62)):

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `indexed_sha` | the snapshot that answered; `<sha>+dirty` when it was built from uncommitted work |
| `head_sha` | the live HEAD, or `unknown` when git cannot answer |
| `dirty` | whether the working tree has indexable changes |
| `stale`, `stale_reason` | whether the answer lags the checkout: `head_moved`, `working_tree_dirty`, `working_tree_changed` or `working_tree_reverted`. Omitted, never `false`, when git cannot answer |
| `refresh` | `none` on a clean tree; `started` when this answer queued a refresh (with `refresh_target`); `completed` on answers from the refreshed snapshot in the next 10 minutes (with `refresh_snapshot` and `refreshed_at`) |

A stale answer is still an answer: it tells the assistant the line numbers may
have moved. A long-running MCP server queues the refresh itself and says so
with `refresh: "started"`.

## Controlling Token Spend

Tune detail and format so results fit the assistant's context window instead
of trimming after the fact:

- Use `detail=low` when you only need counts or minimal metadata; `medium` for
  names and signatures; `high` for repository-local evidence; `xhigh` only
  when broader cross-repo context is required. Since 0.1.55 the tool schema's
  `detail` enum lists every accepted spelling (`l`/`0`, `med`/`m`/`1`,
  `h`/`2`, `x`/`max`/`full`/`3`), and each means what it means on the CLI and
  the HTTP API ([#146](https://github.com/aziron-ai/atlas/issues/146)).
- Use `format=plain` for compact line-oriented output when the client does not
  need structured JSON.
- Set `max_tokens` to bound a `code_query` answer; an answer trimmed to fit is
  marked `truncated:true`. Strict budget mode refuses an oversized answer and
  returns `budget_exceeded` instead.

## Transport Security

Stdio MCP is local to the launching assistant. HTTP MCP should stay on
loopback unless authentication and origin restrictions are configured:

```sh
export ATLAS_API_TOKEN='replace-with-a-strong-token'
export ATLAS_MCP_ALLOWED_ORIGINS='https://trusted.example'
atlas serve --mcp --addr 0.0.0.0:3099
```

See [Privacy and Data Handling](privacy) before enabling networked access, and
[Dashboard and HTTP API](service) for the full service surface.

---

# CLI Reference
URL: https://atlas.aziro.com/docs/cli/

# CLI Reference

Every Atlas capability is a subcommand of the single `atlas` binary. This page
is the complete map: global flags first, then each command grouped by task,
with worked examples. For narrative guides, start with
[Getting Started](getting-started) and [Indexing and Reindexing](indexing).

## Global Flags

These flags apply to every command and control which database answers, which
repo is in scope, and how output is shaped.

| Flag | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `--db` | Storage DSN: `sqlite://PATH` or `postgres://...` (default `sqlite://./.atlas/atlas.db`). |
| `--detail` | Output depth: `low`, `medium`, `high`, or `xhigh` — how much graph context to return per item. Default `high` for every format; `xhigh` opts into cross-repo context. Retrieval ops (callers/refs/impact) floor at `high`. |
| `--format` | Output shape: `plain`, `json`, `compact`, or `ndjson` (`json` by default). |
| `--json` | Shorthand for `--format json`. |
| `--read-only` | Open the database read-only: no migration, no writes or checkpoints, no `telemetry.db` created beside it, and no `-wal`/`-shm` beside a quiescent store — artifact bytes hash identically after any query. Since 0.1.55 it follows a live writer: once a running Atlas has a WAL beside the store it reads it, and it refuses a store moved to another schema generation (`store_superseded`) ([#130](https://github.com/aziron-ai/atlas/issues/130)). A missing database errors instead of being created. |
| `--repo` | Repo workspace: path, `org/name`, or repo_id. Defaults to the current directory; `'*'` means all repos on `search`/`semantic-search`. |
| `--telemetry-db` | Explicit path for the observability database — required if you want telemetry with `--read-only`. Default: `telemetry.db` beside the graph database. |
| `--tenant` | Tenant/org scope to isolate repos to (hosted multi-tenant; empty = all repos). |

Combine them freely with any command:

```sh
atlas --repo /absolute/path status
atlas --db "sqlite:///absolute/path/.atlas/atlas.db" --format plain stats
atlas --detail xhigh explain NewServer
atlas --repo '*' search "rate limiter"
```

### How a Workspace Finds Its Index

A workspace-scoped command answers in two steps: which store, then which
repository in it. The store is the `--db` you typed, else a running server
(`ATLAS_SERVER_URL`, or a local `atlas serve` on `127.0.0.1:3099`), else
`./.atlas/atlas.db`. Inside the store an explicit `--repo` wins, then the
registered root that contains the path.

**Since 0.1.55**, a git checkout that no registered root contains — a linked
worktree, another clone, a worktree of a bare clone — is served by an existing
index when it shares that repository's git common directory or normalized
`origin` URL, and its HEAD and working-tree state equal the repository's
latest snapshot ([#42](https://github.com/aziron-ai/atlas/issues/42)).
`atlas status --repo <path>` then reports `repo_scope.workspace_reuse` and the
line `workspace <path> served by the index of <root>`.

A checkout with the same identity but different content is refused with
`verdict: content_differs` rather than served stale line numbers, a copy that
is not a git checkout is never matched (`not_a_git_checkout`), and several
equal checkouts are `ambiguous_repo` with `candidates[]`. Every refusal names
the `searched_stores` and the `checkout` diagnosis. To read an index
explicitly, pin it with `atlas --db <dsn> --repo <repo_id>`.

## Index and Health

Build the graph, keep it fresh, and verify that storage and schema are sound.

| Command | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `index` | Index a repo: parse symbols, edges, and routes; persist the graph and lexical index. Incremental by default; `--reindex` forces a full rebuild; `--workers N` (or `ATLAS_INDEX_WORKERS`; 0 = all cores) caps the parse/hash pool and overrides whatever the machine profile would set. Since 0.1.48, `--format json` also reports `persist_mode`, `persist_path`, `files_reparsed`, `lexical_bytes`, and `lexical_settle`. |
| `watch` | Index once, then watch the working tree and apply debounced incremental updates on every file change. Foreground until interrupted. |
| `status` | Storage and version health: schema/index-format contracts and per-repo snapshot format state (`--schema` for contract versions and drift). Since 0.1.55 `--repo` scopes the whole report to one repo, and the report carries a `telemetry` block. |
| `stats` | Graph and index telemetry statistics for an indexed repo. Since 0.1.55 it names its count projections, checks seven `invariants` between them, and carries graph-health fields and a `telemetry` block. |
| `doctor` | Report upgrade health and schema/index contract state; `--verify` also checks whether the `atlas` on PATH matches the running binary; `--deep` runs a page-level integrity scan (`PRAGMA quick_check`) to catch on-disk corruption reads silently tolerate. Since 0.1.48 it also reports a `machine_profile` block — the detected tier, the probe facts behind it, `cpu_width_scope`, and every bound actually installed. |
| `report` | Compose graph stats, top hubs, and top communities; `--format plain` prints the Markdown report directly. Since 0.1.55 it lists clusters only and prints graph-health warnings and coverage tables. |
| `migrate` | Apply storage migrations and report the active contracts. |
| `compact` | Reclaim space and truncate the WAL; `--full` also runs a full VACUUM and rebuilds an oversized lexical sidecar; `--rebuild-lexical` fixes an empty or wedged sidecar. |
| `link` | Register a repo into the graph without indexing it, so it joins cross-repo queries and appears in `status`. Idempotent. |
| `repo` | Repo registry maintenance — `repo rm` forgets a repo: snapshots, symbols, edges, embeddings, and lexical docs. |

```sh
atlas index . --enable-vectors
atlas watch .
atlas doctor --verbose
atlas report --format plain
```

### Status, Stats and Telemetry

**Since 0.1.55:**

- `atlas status --repo <path|org/name|repo_id>` scopes the whole report —
  served snapshot, counts, format drift and watch lock — to that repo and adds
  `repo_scope`. An unknown repo is refused exactly as `stats` refuses it, with
  exit code 1. Without `--repo`, or with `--repo '*'`, the global view is
  unchanged ([#155](https://github.com/aziron-ai/atlas/issues/155)).
- `atlas stats` names its four count projections (`latest`, `store_rows`,
  `graph.raw_*`, `graph`) and checks seven `invariants` between them: `ok`,
  `partial` when the graph was not computed at this scale, or `violated` with
  the failing checks named. `graph.edge_binding` accounts for every edge row
  on its way into `graph.edges`, including rows bound to several targets
  (`multi_bound_rows`) ([#14](https://github.com/aziron-ai/atlas/issues/14)).
- `stats`, `status` and `doctor` carry a `telemetry` block — `available`,
  `unavailable_read_only`, `unavailable`, `stale` or `missing`, with `reason`
  and `remedy` — and plain output prints a `telemetry` line whenever it is not
  `available` ([#154](https://github.com/aziron-ai/atlas/issues/154)).

```text
  edge_binding  raw 3 = graph-kind 2 + other 1;  graph-kind = bound 1 + unresolved 1;  multi-bound 0;  pairs 1 -> edges 1 (collapsed 0)
  invariants ok  (7 checked)
  telemetry unavailable_read_only  sink not_attached  index_run present
```

## Search and Retrieval

Find code and pull bounded, deterministic context about it.

| Command | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `search` | Code-aware lexical search (BM25 + trigram) over the symbol index; `--mode lexical\|semantic\|hybrid`, plus `--kind` and `--path` filters. Since 0.1.55 equal scores are ordered by path, name, kind, signature and line, so every fresh index returns the same page ([#135](https://github.com/aziron-ai/atlas/issues/135)). |
| `semantic-search` | Embedding-based nearest-symbol search; transparently degrades to lexical (`degraded=true`) when vectors are unavailable. |
| `context` | Bounded review-context bundle for changed/seed paths; budgets via `--intent` (`auto` is 16-32 KiB), per-request flags, or env vars. |
| `explain` | Deterministic context bundle for a symbol: defs, callers/callees, imports, served routes, cross-repo consumers. |
| `symbol` | Show a symbol's definition(s) with its callers and callees. |
| `snippet` | Show a symbol's bounded implementation body (path:line, signature, source excerpt). |
| `callers` | List symbols that directly call a symbol; scope overloaded names with `--package`, `--receiver`, or `--arity`. Since 0.1.55 the answer leads with `caller_names`, and `--brief` keeps the whole caller list with less detail per caller. |
| `refs` | List references to a symbol: call sites plus type-use references (params, fields, returns). Since 0.1.55 `--mutations` (alias `--writes`) lists only the references that write the symbol ([#55](https://github.com/aziron-ai/atlas/issues/55)). |
| `neighbors` | Depth-1 call neighborhood: a symbol's direct callers and callees. |
| `path` | Shortest forward call path from one symbol to another (`--max-depth`, default 6). |

```sh
atlas search "authentication middleware" --mode lexical --format plain
atlas context --paths internal/api/handler.go --intent review \
  --query "review correctness and regression risk"
atlas callers NewServer --limit 50 --receiver '*Server'
atlas path Handler ServeHTTP --max-depth 6
```

Use `search` for discovery; use `context` when reviewing changed paths and you
need bounded related code; use `explain`/`symbol` when you already know the
symbol.

## Graph Analysis

Measure blast radius, contracts, structure, and change over time.

| Command | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `impact` | Single-repo blast radius for a change: impacted symbols, files, and tests (`--tests` on by default). |
| `cross-repo-impact` | Cross-repo blast radius: which other repos call routes the changed handlers serve. |
| `consumers` | Other repos that call any route this repo serves. |
| `dependencies` | Producer repos/handlers that serve HTTP calls this repo makes. |
| `route-contracts` | The producer HTTP routes a repo serves — its public contract. |
| `coverage` | Real covered/total line ratio when a runtime profile was imported (`coverage import`); otherwise static call-graph reachability. |
| `hubs` | Rank the graph's hubs ("god nodes") by call-graph degree centrality. Since 0.1.55 degree-zero symbols are never hubs (see Graph Health below). |
| `communities` | Detect deterministic clusters of densely connected symbols; since 0.1.55 identical across fresh indexes of one commit, with isolated symbols flagged. |
| `history` | Per-commit snapshot timeline for a repo; since 0.1.55 a snapshot built from uncommitted work is its own row, labelled `<sha>+dirty`. |
| `snapshot-diff` | Structural diff between two snapshots: symbols/edges added, removed, modified (alias: `diff`). `--from`/`--to` take a commit sha, a snapshot id, or since 0.1.55 `<sha>+dirty`. |
| `export` | Export the call graph as `json`, `mermaid`, `dot`, or a self-contained interactive `html` page; `--bundle DIR` writes graph.html plus report.md. |

```sh
atlas impact --paths internal/api/handler.go --max-depth 3
atlas cross-repo-impact --paths internal/api/handler.go
atlas consumers --max-staleness-days 30
atlas export --symbol NewServer --depth 2 --format html -o graph.html
```

Cross-repository results depend on linked repositories and indexed service
contracts — see `atlas link` above.

## Freshness on Every Answer

**Since 0.1.55**, every repo-scoped answer — `search`, `symbol`, `callers`,
`refs`, `impact`, `context`, `explain`, `snippet` — says how its snapshot
relates to the checkout, with the same fields on MCP and the HTTP API
([#59](https://github.com/aziron-ai/atlas/issues/59)):

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `indexed_sha` | the snapshot that answered; `<sha>+dirty` when it was built from uncommitted work |
| `head_sha` | the live HEAD, or `unknown` when git cannot answer |
| `dirty` | whether the working tree has indexable changes |
| `stale`, `stale_reason` | whether the answer lags the checkout, and why: `head_moved`, `working_tree_dirty`, `working_tree_changed` or `working_tree_reverted`. Omitted, never `false`, when git cannot answer |
| `refresh`, `refresh_skipped` | what Atlas did about it: `none`, `started` or `completed`; a one-shot command reports `refresh_skipped: "one_shot"` |

Plain output opens with a notice when an answer is stale:

```text
stale: indexed 4fb9d0f74f1c vs head 4fb9d0f74f1c+dirty  (working_tree_dirty)  not refreshed (one-shot command; run `atlas index`)
```

A one-shot command (anything but `serve`, `mcp` and `watch`) never starts
background index work, because the process would exit before it landed
([#141](https://github.com/aziron-ai/atlas/issues/141)). Refresh with
`atlas index`, or set `ATLAS_ONESHOT_REFRESH=sync` to re-index a git-stale
repo before answering, bounded by `ATLAS_ONESHOT_REFRESH_TIMEOUT` (default
10s); an overrun reports `refresh_skipped: "budget_exceeded"` and persists
nothing. The check costs one HEAD read and one `git status` of the indexable
files per repo, reused for `ATLAS_FRESHNESS_TTL` (default 2s);
`ATLAS_FRESHNESS_PROBE=0` turns it off.

## Graph Health

**Since 0.1.55**, `hubs`, `communities`, `report` and `stats` describe how
connected the graph is, so a sparse graph is not mistaken for an
architecture ([#45](https://github.com/aziron-ai/atlas/issues/45),
[#149](https://github.com/aziron-ai/atlas/issues/149)):

- `hubs` ranks only symbols with at least one resolved call or inheritance
  relation and reports `eligible`, `excluded_isolated`, `ranking` and
  `warnings`; on a sparse graph the list is shorter than `--limit`.
- `communities` is deterministic: one commit gives the same partition, ids
  and order on every fresh index and at any `--workers` count. `total` splits
  into `multi_member` and `singletons`, and isolated one-symbol communities
  are flagged.
- `report` lists clusters only, counts isolated symbols in its summary, and
  prints `WARNING:` lines and relation-coverage tables by language and by
  symbol kind.
- `stats` (under `graph`) and `report` carry `isolated_ratio`,
  `connected_components`, `largest_component`, `multi_member_communities`,
  `singleton_communities`, relation coverage and `warnings`.

| Warning | Fires when |
| --- | --- |
| `isolated_majority` | at least half the symbols have no resolved relation |
| `fragmented_communities` | the connected symbols split into communities of two or fewer on average (evaluated with a computed partition and at least 20 connected symbols) |

On a three-function repository where one function calls nothing and nothing
calls it:

```text
$ atlas hubs --format plain
hubs  total 2  eligible 2  excluded_isolated 1
  helper  function  in 1  out 0  total 1  main.go
  main  function  in 0  out 1  total 1  main.go

$ atlas communities --format plain
communities  total 2  shown 2  multi_member 1  singletons 1  isolated 1
  #0  size 2  helper, main
  #1  size 1  extra  (isolated)
```

## Assistants and Surfaces

Wire Atlas into AI assistants and serve it over MCP or HTTP. See
[MCP Tools](mcp) and [Dashboard and HTTP API](service).

| Command | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `bootstrap` | Register Atlas as an MCP server and install the atlas-first skill and CLAUDE.md directive for all detected assistants (Claude desktop+CLI, Codex, Copilot, Cursor, Gemini). Idempotent. |
| `install` | Install integration glue piecemeal: `install skill` (assistant registration), `install hook` (git hook that keeps the graph fresh), `install aziron`. |
| `uninstall` | Reverse `bootstrap` across every assistant it provisions; touches only atlas-managed entries. `--purge` also deletes the `.atlas` index databases (global `~/.atlas` + registry repo roots), showing the blast radius and requiring `--yes` (or `--dry-run`). Idempotent. |
| `mcp` | Expose graph/search/impact as MCP tools over stdio (default), Streamable HTTP (`--http`), or legacy SSE (`--sse`); `--supervise` runs the warm gateway. |
| `serve` | Run the REST HTTP API and dashboard on `127.0.0.1:3099`; `--mcp` also mounts MCP over HTTP at `POST /mcp`. |
| `skill` | Author, test, render, and distribute runbook skills (`new`, `lint`, `test`, `register`, `render`, `push`, `pull`, and more). |

```sh
atlas bootstrap --dry-run
atlas install skill --agent codex,claude,claude-desktop
atlas mcp --supervise
atlas serve --mcp
```

Both `mcp` and `serve` watch the repo by default to keep the graph fresh;
disable with `--watch=false` or `ATLAS_NO_WATCH=1`.

## Fleet and Org

Connect a machine to a central Atlas server and share telemetry or trusted
automations. See [Privacy and Data Handling](privacy) for what leaves the
machine at each data level.

| Command | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `connect` | Register this machine with the central Atlas server under a stable device identity and install capture hooks; `--level off\|telemetry\|interactions\|full` governs what is shared (default `interactions`). |
| `disconnect` | Disconnect from the central Atlas and remove capture hooks. |
| `sync` | Fleet telemetry uplink: `sync status` shows configuration, kill switches, and cursors; `sync now` pushes all pending telemetry once. |
| `recall` | Frequent-prompt mining, replayable automations, and org sync (`clusters`, `promote`, `push`, `pull`, `state`, and more). |

```sh
atlas connect https://atlas.example.com --level interactions
atlas sync status
atlas recall clusters
```

## Utilities

| Command | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `config` | Inspect and persist configuration: `list` every knob with effective value and provenance, `get` one, `set` one into the workspace settings.json. See [Configuration](configuration). |
| `version` | Print the installed Atlas version. |
| `completion` | Generate shell completion scripts. |

```sh
atlas config list
atlas config get ATLAS_MAX_DB_BYTES
```

## Maintenance Safety

Stop long-running Atlas processes (`serve`, `watch`, supervised MCP) before
exclusive maintenance such as `compact --full`. Back up the complete `.atlas/`
directory before destructive operations like `repo rm`:

```sh
atlas migrate
atlas compact --full
atlas repo rm owner/repository --yes
```

## Authoritative Contract

Flags and defaults can change between releases. `atlas --help` and
`atlas <command> --help` are the authoritative contract for the release
installed on your machine; prefer them over this page when they disagree.

---

# Indexing and Reindexing
URL: https://atlas.aziro.com/docs/indexing/

# Indexing and Reindexing

Atlas answers are only as current as the selected index. This guide covers
creating and updating an index, forcing a rebuild, keeping the graph fresh
automatically, controlling what gets indexed, and maintaining the database
that stores it. For what the graph contains, see [Core Concepts](concepts).

## Create or Update an Index

Run this once to build the graph, and again whenever you want to refresh it —
the same command handles both cases. From a repository root:

```sh
atlas index .
```

To pin an explicit database instead of the default `sqlite://./.atlas/atlas.db`:

```sh
atlas --db "sqlite:///absolute/path/.atlas/atlas.db" index .
```

`atlas index` parses symbols, edges, and routes, then persists the graph and
the lexical search index. By default it indexes the working tree; use
`--ref COMMIT_OR_BRANCH` to index a specific commit or branch instead.

**Since 0.1.55, uncommitted work gets a snapshot of its own.** When the
working tree has uncommitted edits or untracked files that Atlas indexes, the
run stores a snapshot labelled `<sha>+dirty`, with a `tree_hash` of the dirty
paths and their content, beside the clean snapshot of that commit instead of
overwriting it. The index JSON reports `dirty`, `tree_hash` and `indexed_sha`,
and `status`, `history`, `snapshots list` and `snapshot-diff` show the label.
A clean re-index of the same commit still replaces its snapshot in place, and
committing the work stores the new commit's snapshot. Files Atlas never reads
(its own `.atlas/`, extensions it does not index, `.atlasignore` matches)
never make a tree dirty. `ATLAS_INDEX_DIRTY_IDENTITY=0` restores the old
behaviour of labelling the working tree with the clean commit
([#65](https://github.com/aziron-ai/atlas/issues/65)).

A first index of inference-gateway, a Go service of 307 files, looks like this
on stderr (the JSON summary goes to stdout):

```text
atlas index: starting path=. db=sqlite://…/.atlas/atlas.db
atlas index: analyzing types (307 files, 11092 symbols) elapsed=2s
…
atlas index: analyzing types (307 files, 11092 symbols) elapsed=24s
atlas index: persisting 11092 symbols elapsed=26s
atlas index: done repo=inference-gateway mode=full files=307 symbols=11092 edges=13900 routes=71 duration=27014ms
atlas index: timings build_symbols_edges=25539ms … go_types=25510ms lexical=795ms lexical_settle=132ms log_sites=9ms parse=115ms persist=438ms …
```

On a Go repository most of a cold index is Go type analysis (`go_types`); the
parse itself took 115 ms here.

## What Index Output Reports

Read the index output to confirm what actually happened rather than assuming.
With `--progress` (on by default for human output), Atlas prints start,
periodic progress, and completion statistics to stderr. A run reports a delta
update when files changed, or a no-op when the stored snapshot already
matches the workspace. For profiling an index run, `--cpuprofile PATH` and
`--memprofile PATH` write runtime/pprof profiles.

**Since 0.1.48, `atlas index --format json` also reports what the run did
internally**, so you can verify the fast paths engaged instead of inferring it
from a stopwatch:

```json
{
  "mode": "delta",
  "persist_mode": "delta",
  "persist_path": "sql",
  "delta_base": "dc4dc4ba86e307b8875a4c0b0623b628445d6274",
  "files_reparsed": 1,
  "lexical_bytes": 290368,
  "lexical_settle": "merged"
}
```

| Field | Values | What it tells you |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `persist_mode` | `full`, `delta`, `noop` | which mode the run resolved to. `noop` means the working tree already matched the stored snapshot |
| `persist_path` | `sql`, `sql_new_commit`, `whole_graph`, `full_walk`, `full_stream`, `noop` | the decisive one. `sql` and `sql_new_commit` are the O(change) paths — the base graph is never loaded into memory. `whole_graph` is the correctness fallback: a delta by mode, a full index by memory |
| `delta_base`, `delta_base_snapshot` | commit SHA, snapshot id | which snapshot the run built on, so a ladder of runs is pinnable |
| `files_reparsed` | integer | defined for every mode: changed plus added on a delta, every indexed file on a full run, `0` on a no-op |
| `lexical_bytes` | integer | the on-disk size of `.atlas/lexical` after the run settled it. This should match a `du` taken the instant `index` returns; a mismatch is a bug report, not a measurement |
| `lexical_settle` | see below | how the sidecar reached the size reported in `lexical_bytes` |

### Lexical Settle States

The lexical (BM25) sidecar writes new segments and supersedes old ones
asynchronously, so a footprint measured the moment an index returns used to
read far above the steady state. Since 0.1.48 `atlas index` settles the
sidecar before it returns — a bounded segment merge, then a reclaiming reopen
— and reports how that went. The settle never changes the document set and
never fails a run; every failure mode degrades to a disclosed state.

| State | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `merged` | the merge completed and superseded segments were reclaimed. **Only this state asserts a steady-state footprint** |
| `reclaimed` | the merge was skipped or declined, but the reclaim ran. Superseded segments are gone; unmerged ones may remain |
| `partial` | **Since 0.1.51.** Every step ran and reported success, and then the check found the sidecar still holding obsolete document bytes a compaction would reclaim — a contended machine can leave a whole superseded generation inside one segment, which the engine declines to re-merge. The reported footprint is **above** steady state. Re-run on a quiet machine, or run `atlas compact --rebuild-lexical`, before quoting a size |
| `timeout` | the merge did not finish inside its budget, so the reclaim was deliberately not attempted and the footprint may hold both unmerged and superseded segments. Raise `ATLAS_LEXICAL_SETTLE_TIMEOUT` (default 30s) and re-run |
| `skipped` | there was nothing to settle: no sidecar, or this run wrote no documents |
| `failed` | the settle itself errored; the reason is on stderr and the footprint is still reported |
| `off` | disabled with `ATLAS_LEXICAL_SETTLE=off` |

Set `ATLAS_LEXICAL_SETTLE=reclaim` to skip the merge and only reclaim — the
cheaper mode for very large sidecars where a single-segment merge is not worth
its write amplification.

Running the same command again on an unchanged tree is a no-op — this is the
real second run on inference-gateway, trimmed:

```text
$ atlas index . --format json
{
  "repo_full_name": "inference-gateway",
  "commit_sha": "524967508e9d90185c4a1c3540cac0dcda7c580a",
  "indexed_files": 307,
  "symbols": 11092,
  "edges": 13900,
  "routes": 71,
  "mode": "noop",
  "duration_ms": 69,
  "persist_mode": "noop",
  "persist_path": "noop",
  "delta_base": "524967508e9d90185c4a1c3540cac0dcda7c580a",
  "files_reparsed": 0,
  "lexical_bytes": 6991343,
  "lexical_settle": "merged"
}
```

## Incremental Behavior

Incremental updates are the default because they are much faster than full
rebuilds: Atlas computes a delta against the previous snapshot and reindexes
only what changed. To diff against a specific commit rather than the stored
base, pass `--base COMMIT`.

**Since 0.1.55, a new commit costs what it changed.** The lexical sidecar is
carried forward per snapshot, so a new commit re-streams only the changed
files' documents, and the shapes that used to rebuild the whole graph — adding
or deleting JS/TS, Python, C, C++ or Rust files, deleting a Go file, turning
Go type analysis off, fact-changing header edits — run on the SQL delta path
(`persist_path: sql_new_commit`) with bounded passes after the commit
([#128](https://github.com/aziron-ai/atlas/issues/128)). A delta and a fresh
full index of the same commit hold identical symbols, edges and file rows
([#118](https://github.com/aziron-ai/atlas/issues/118)).

Because uncommitted work is now its own snapshot, an edit to a dirty tree
takes that same new-commit path (copy forward, then retire the superseded
dirty snapshot) instead of rewriting a snapshot in place. Watch mode on a large
repository therefore pays roughly what a new commit costs for each edit; set
`ATLAS_INDEX_DIRTY_IDENTITY=0` if that matters more than an honest label
([#65](https://github.com/aziron-ai/atlas/issues/65)).

## Imports and Cross-File Types

Atlas proves which file a name comes from before it counts a cross-file
relationship, and fails closed when two files could answer. **Since 0.1.55**
the proof reaches further:

- **Python.** `from X import A, B` keeps the module row plus one row per
  binding, marked `import_binding` / `import_module`, and `export` folds the
  bindings onto one edge per statement. Parenthesized imports are read from
  the syntax tree, and `from . import foo` stores `.foo`
  ([#126](https://github.com/aziron-ai/atlas/issues/126)).
- **Go.** Imports resolve through `go.mod` — nested modules and in-repo
  `replace` directives included — to the package directory
  (`resolved_kind: package_dir`); an in-module path with no package is marked
  `module_not_found`, and the standard library and third-party modules fail
  closed. A delta refreshes the resolution when a package directory is added
  or removed or `go.mod` changes
  ([#126](https://github.com/aziron-ai/atlas/issues/126)). Package-level
  variables carry their initializer call, their writes and an inferred
  `declared_type` ([#55](https://github.com/aziron-ai/atlas/issues/55)).
- **Scala.** Each import selector resolves by Scala's lookup order and gains
  `resolved_path` only when exactly one file declares the target under a
  verified package clause ([#137](https://github.com/aziron-ai/atlas/issues/137));
  type uses, universal `apply` and companions resolve through the same imports
  ([#21](https://github.com/aziron-ai/atlas/issues/21)).
- **PHP.** `use` clauses are read per namespace region, one row per clause,
  so grouped and aliased imports prove their class, and `use function` /
  `use const` resolve only to functions and constants
  ([#139](https://github.com/aziron-ai/atlas/issues/139)). Class constants,
  static properties, container and event rows prove their class too
  ([#24](https://github.com/aziron-ai/atlas/issues/24)).
- **Java.** Same-package, single-type and on-demand imports resolve type
  uses, and method return types, field types and annotation element types
  are references ([#34](https://github.com/aziron-ai/atlas/issues/34)).

These facts are written when a file is indexed, so an existing store shows
them after one `atlas index . --reindex`.

## Images

An image is a searchable file-level entry, never a call-graph node. **Since
0.1.55** its entry holds the text the file itself carries — PNG text chunks
(including XMP) and EXIF, JPEG EXIF/XMP/IPTC/comments, TIFF text tags, WebP
EXIF/XMP and GIF comments — plus its format and size, so a title or caption
embedded in an image is found by search
([#26](https://github.com/aziron-ai/atlas/issues/26)). Binary data is never
read as text.

Text drawn in the pixels needs OCR, which is opt-in. Set
`ATLAS_IMAGE_OCR_CMD` to a command that reads one image on stdin and prints
its text; it runs without a shell, with the repo-relative path in
`ATLAS_IMAGE_PATH`, for at most 30 s per image:

```sh
export ATLAS_IMAGE_OCR_CMD="tesseract - stdout"
atlas index . --reindex
```

Every image entry states `ocr_status` (`off`, `ok`, `empty`, `unavailable` or
`failed`), and its signature says `ocr: <status>` whenever no OCR text was
indexed, for example `fixture.png png 320x60 ocr: off Title: ATLAS VISION
TOKEN 7842`. Images already indexed keep their text until they are indexed
again with `--reindex`.

## Forced Rebuild

Use `--reindex` only when the incremental path cannot repair the index:

```sh
atlas index . --reindex
```

The legitimate reasons for a full rebuild are:

1. An upgrade reports an incompatible or stale index format, or
   `atlas doctor` recommends a rebuild.
2. Parser or language support changed and old files must be reparsed.
3. The workspace identity or indexed root was incorrect, or focused
   troubleshooting confirms the current index is incomplete.

Do not make forced reindexing the default workflow. It is slower and discards
the benefit of incremental updates.

## Watch Mode

Use watch mode when you want the graph to stay fresh during active editing
with no manual `atlas index` runs. `atlas watch` indexes the repo once, then
watches the working tree and runs an incremental, working-tree-aware update on
every file change. A burst of edits is coalesced into one update
(`--debounce-ms`, default 250). It runs in the foreground until interrupted.

```sh
atlas watch .
```

The MCP and HTTP surfaces maintain freshness the same way — `atlas mcp` and
`atlas serve` watch the repo by default. Disable watching when another process
owns indexing:

```sh
atlas mcp --supervise --watch=false   # or set ATLAS_NO_WATCH=1
```

## Semantic Vectors (Optional)

Enable vectors only if you want embedding-based retrieval; the deterministic
lexical and graph core never depends on them. Run the optional embedding pass
at index time:

```sh
atlas index . --enable-vectors
atlas watch . --enable-vectors   # keep embeddings fresh on each update
```

With vectors enabled (`ATLAS_ENABLE_VECTORS=1` and a repo indexed with
`--enable-vectors`), `atlas semantic-search` returns nearest symbols by cosine
similarity. Otherwise it transparently degrades to lexical search and reports
`degraded=true` / `mode_used=lexical`. By default the embedder is offline
(deterministic token overlap); set `ATLAS_EMBED_URL` to use a real embedding
model. See [Configuration](configuration).

## Excluding Files

Exclude generated outputs, dependency caches, and nested repository snapshots
so they do not pollute search results. Atlas skips paths git ignores by
default (`--gitignore`, default true); pass `--gitignore=false` to index
everything. Add Atlas-specific patterns to:

```text
.atlasignore
```

## Registering Without Indexing

Use `atlas link` when a repo should participate in cross-repo queries and
appear in `atlas status` before (or without) being indexed on this machine:

```sh
atlas link org/name --branch main
```

`REPO` may be a filesystem path, a git remote URL, or a bare `org/name`.
Linking is idempotent — re-linking updates the registration and reports
`created=false`. Linking does not populate the graph; run `atlas index` for
that. To remove a repo from the registry, `atlas repo rm` forgets it entirely:
snapshots, symbols, edges, embeddings, and lexical documents.

## Performance Envelope

**Since 0.1.48, resource use is a profile decision first.** Atlas detects a
machine profile — `eco`, `balanced`, `performance`, or `turbo` — and sizes
indexing to it. The individual knobs below all still work and all still win
over the tier; they are overrides, not the primary control. Pin a tier with
`ATLAS_PROFILE` and read back what it installed with `atlas doctor`; the
tiers, their values, and the auto-detection rules are in
[Configuration](configuration).

Since 0.1.51, the one rule that matters most while indexing is: **`balanced` bounds background
work, not the index you are waiting on.** A watch-triggered refresh or an MCP
lazy index runs inside a warm daemon and takes 3/4 of the cores under a
`RAM/4` soft heap limit; an explicit `atlas index` you typed runs at full
width with no ceiling. `eco` is deliberately not scoped that way — on a
genuinely low-spec box it throttles foreground indexes too, because that is
the case it exists to protect.

Behaviors worth knowing on large or memory-constrained machines:

- **Streaming index (v0.1.42+).** Full indexes of repos over ~15,000 candidate
  files automatically stream in bounded batches instead of holding the whole
  graph in memory — the Linux kernel (81k files, 1.86M symbols, 6.8M edges)
  indexes at ~1.3 GiB peak RSS. Force it at any size with
  `ATLAS_STREAM_INDEX=1` (or off with `0`); tune with
  `ATLAS_STREAM_INDEX_THRESHOLD` and `ATLAS_STREAM_INDEX_BATCH`.
- **CPU ceiling (v0.1.43+; an override since 0.1.48).** With no profile bound
  in force the parse/hash pool uses all cores, so a large index can saturate
  the machine (a Chromium index drove one reporter's CPU past 300%). Cap it
  explicitly with `atlas index --workers N` or `ATLAS_INDEX_WORKERS` — e.g.
  `--workers 4` trades a little wall-time for headroom, and `1` pins the run
  to a single core. An explicit value always beats the tier's worker count.
  (Go repos also run `go/types`, which spawns its own compilers outside this
  pool; C/C++/other tree-sitter languages are fully bounded by it.)
- **Memory ceiling (an override since 0.1.48).** `ATLAS_MEMORY_LIMIT` and
  `ATLAS_GOGC` bound the Go runtime directly and override whatever the tier
  would have set — the right tool for a container with a hard cgroup limit,
  where you want a specific number rather than a fraction of host RAM.
- **Deletions no longer rebuild the graph (since 0.1.55).** Deleting a Go
  file used to force the whole-module type-check fallback, and adding or
  deleting JS/TS or Python files took the whole-graph path. Those shapes now
  run on the SQL delta path: on TensorFlow a one-line Python edit went from
  1,528 MB / 36 s to 529 MB / 13 s, and adding a `.cc` file beside JavaScript
  from 8.5 GB / 184 s to 752 MB / 24 s
  ([#128](https://github.com/aziron-ai/atlas/issues/128)). Under `eco`, SQLite's
  caches and memory map are bounded as well (see [Configuration](configuration)).

## Database Maintenance

Run maintenance when the database has grown or after an Atlas upgrade.

- `atlas compact` reports reclaimable pages and truncates the WAL. Modern
  Atlas databases use online incremental auto-vacuum; legacy databases are
  converted with a one-time full VACUUM that takes an exclusive lock — stop
  `atlas serve` and watch processes first, or you get a lock error rather
  than partial work.
- `atlas compact --full` additionally runs a full VACUUM and rebuilds the
  lexical (BM25) sidecar when it has outgrown its size bound — the only way
  dead segments are returned to the OS. Exclusive: quiesce other Atlas
  processes first.
- `atlas compact --rebuild-lexical` rebuilds the lexical sidecar regardless of
  size — the fix for an empty or wedged sidecar, which otherwise silently
  degrades every search to SQL-only. `atlas doctor` reports when you need it.
- `atlas migrate` applies storage migrations and reports the active contracts.
  Both `migrate` and `compact` accept `--all --root DIR` to process every
  local `.atlas/atlas.db` under a directory.

## Verify Freshness

Confirm which index is answering before trusting results:

```sh
atlas status
atlas stats
atlas doctor
```

When multiple repositories or databases exist, pin both `--db` and `--repo`.
If a running Atlas server is configured, CLI queries may use that server —
unset `ATLAS_SERVER_URL` or pin an explicit database while diagnosing.

```text
$ atlas stats
stats inference-gateway  local/sqlite  history 1  coverage_facts 0
  latest 52496750  mode full  files 307  symbols 11092  edges 13900  routes 71  53534ms
  store_rows files 307  symbols 11092  edges 13900  routes 71
  graph files 89  symbols 3526  edges 1317  communities 3161  isolated 3121
  langs  go:3511 bash:9 typescript:6
```

Since 0.1.55 the plain `stats` output also prints a `health` line (isolated
ratio, connected components, the community split), an `edge_binding` line and
an `invariants` line, and `atlas status --repo <path>` scopes the status
report to one repository; the [CLI reference](cli) describes each. Every
answer also carries its own `indexed_sha`, `head_sha` and `stale` fields, so
a lookup tells you when the index lags the checkout
([#59](https://github.com/aziron-ai/atlas/issues/59)).

`store_rows` is what the index stored. `graph` is what the graph report reads —
the same numbers the dashboard's **Orientation** view (`#/orient`) shows at the
top, beside the repository's entry points and its most-connected symbols:

![Orientation for inference-gateway: 89 files, 3,526 symbols, 1,317 edges, 3,161 communities, 3,121 isolated, a language bar, entry points and load-bearing symbols](assets/docs/indexing/orientation-index-state.png "Orientation reads the graph report of the selected repository.")

To walk what was indexed file by file, open **Files** (`#/files`). Type in the
filter to narrow the tree by path or symbol name, then click a file: the
details panel lists the routes it serves, its imports and the symbols in it,
with caller and callee counts.

![The Files view: filtering the indexed tree for routes, then selecting api/routes.go to show its 9 routes, 882 relations and imports](assets/docs/indexing/files-after-index.mp4 "Files after an index: api/routes.go serves 9 routes.")

The counter beside the filter says how much of the index the view loaded. On a
large repository the first load is a sample; expanding a folder fetches that
folder in full.

## Safe Recovery Order

Follow this order so you never destroy data a cheaper step could have fixed:

1. Stop active `serve`, `watch`, and supervised MCP processes.
2. Run `atlas status` and `atlas doctor`.
3. Confirm the repository and database paths.
4. Run `atlas migrate` when a schema upgrade is required.
5. Rebuild lexical data only when recommended.
6. Run `atlas index . --reindex` as the final non-destructive repair.
7. Delete `.atlas` only when a complete data reset is intended.

See [Troubleshooting](troubleshooting) before removing data.

---

# Dashboard and HTTP API
URL: https://atlas.aziro.com/docs/service/

# Dashboard and HTTP API

One `atlas serve` process hosts the local dashboard, the HTTP API, the
repository watcher, and — with `--mcp` — the MCP endpoint. Run it when you
want a browsable view of the graph, when thin clients should share one index,
or when other tooling needs a REST surface.

## Start the Service

Start with MCP mounted so assistants and HTTP clients share the same process:

```sh
atlas serve --mcp
```

Useful variants:

```sh
atlas serve --open        # also auto-open the dashboard in your browser
atlas serve --watch=false  # do not keep the graph fresh in the background
```

Default address and dashboard:

```text
http://127.0.0.1:3099
http://127.0.0.1:3099/dashboard
```

## Serve Flags

| Flag | Default | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--addr` | `127.0.0.1:3099` | Listen address; loopback by default. Use `0.0.0.0:3099` to expose on the network |
| `--mcp` | off | Also mount MCP over HTTP at `POST /mcp` |
| `--open` | `false` | Auto-open the dashboard in your browser once ready (off by default; pass `--open` to enable). `serve` hosts the dashboard either way |
| `--watch` | `true` | Keep the graph fresh by watching the repo; `--watch=false` or `ATLAS_NO_WATCH=1` to disable |
| `--watch-path` | `--repo`, else current dir | Repo path to watch when `--watch` is set |

Global flags such as `--db`, `--repo`, and `--read-only` apply as on any other
command; see the [CLI Reference](cli).

## Health and API Discovery

Use these endpoints to script readiness checks and to discover the API:

```sh
curl http://127.0.0.1:3099/healthz
curl http://127.0.0.1:3099/readyz
curl http://127.0.0.1:3099/openapi.json
```

- `healthz` confirms the process is running.
- `readyz` confirms Atlas can answer a lightweight engine request.
- `openapi.json` is the version-specific API contract. Generate clients and
  validate requests against this document rather than copying request shapes
  from historical examples.

## Common Requests

```sh
curl http://127.0.0.1:3099/api/v1/status
curl http://127.0.0.1:3099/api/v1/stats
curl "http://127.0.0.1:3099/api/v1/search?q=Checkout"
```

The dashboard's Ask Workbench is a route too — a question streams back as
server-sent events, and the threads it keeps are readable and deletable:

```sh
curl -N -X POST http://127.0.0.1:3099/api/v1/ask/workbench \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"question":"what are the auth routes, and who last changed the login one?"}'
curl http://127.0.0.1:3099/api/v1/ask/workbench/threads
```

See [Ask Workbench](workbench) for the stream, the thread routes, the model
providers and the limits.

## Binding Beyond Loopback

Loopback is the safe default. Before binding to another interface, require a
bearer token and restrict browser origins:

```sh
export ATLAS_API_TOKEN='replace-with-a-strong-token'
export ATLAS_MCP_ALLOWED_ORIGINS='https://trusted.example'
atlas serve --mcp --addr 0.0.0.0:3099
```

Authenticated request:

```sh
curl \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $ATLAS_API_TOKEN" \
  http://host:3099/api/v1/status
```

`ATLAS_API_TOKEN` protects `/api/v1/*` and `POST /mcp`. Browser clients from
additional origins must also be explicitly allowed via
`ATLAS_MCP_ALLOWED_ORIGINS`.

When a token-protected dashboard requests credentials, supply the configured
Atlas API token. The dashboard uses authenticated API calls and a short-lived
stream credential for live updates.

### Token Handling

> **Warning:** Do not place the API token in shared links, logs, screenshots,
> or source control. Anyone holding the token can query every repository the
> service indexes.

## TLS

Atlas serves plain HTTP. When traffic leaves the machine, terminate TLS at a
trusted reverse proxy in front of `atlas serve` rather than exposing the
listener directly.

## Service Troubleshooting

Start with Atlas's own diagnostics, then check the port:

```sh
atlas status
atlas doctor
lsof -nP -iTCP:3099 -sTCP:LISTEN
```

If `healthz` passes but `readyz` fails, indexing or database maintenance may
be blocking engine requests. Wait for the current operation or stop competing
Atlas processes before retrying. See [Troubleshooting](troubleshooting) for
broader diagnosis.

---

# Configuration
URL: https://atlas.aziro.com/docs/configuration/

# Configuration

Atlas works with zero configuration on a fresh checkout; every knob has a
compiled default. This page explains where overrides live, which settings
matter most, and the global flags that select storage, scope, and output
shape. For the full command surface, see the [CLI Reference](cli).

## Precedence

Know where a value comes from before changing it. Effective configuration is
resolved in this order (highest wins):

- **Environment variable** — a deployment variable always wins.
- **Repository `.atlas/settings.json`** — stable local policy.
- **Machine profile default** (since 0.1.48) — what the tier in force
  implies for a knob nobody set (see *Machine Profiles* below).
- **Compiled default** — the value Atlas ships with.

Environment variables suit automation and containers; repository settings
suit stable local policy. The profile rung sits below both on purpose: a
profile never overrides a value you set explicitly.

## Inspecting and Persisting Settings

Use `atlas config` to see every knob's effective value and its provenance —
not just what is set, but which layer set it:

```sh
atlas config list                        # every knob, value, and provenance
atlas config get ATLAS_MAX_DB_BYTES      # one knob's value and origin
atlas config set ATLAS_MAX_DB_BYTES 10GiB  # persist into .atlas/settings.json
atlas config set ATLAS_MAX_DB_BYTES ""     # clear a persisted override
```

## Known Settings

The settings most people change, including environment-only variables such as
`ATLAS_API_TOKEN` and `ATLAS_SERVER_URL` that `atlas config` does not list:

| Setting | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `ATLAS_ENABLE_VECTORS` | Enable optional semantic retrieval (pairs with an index built with `--enable-vectors`) |
| `ATLAS_EMBED_URL` | Point semantic search at a real embedding model; the default embedder is offline (deterministic token overlap) |
| `ATLAS_NO_WATCH` | Disable background file watching in `mcp` and `serve` (equivalent to `--watch=false`) |
| `ATLAS_WATCH_MODE` | Select the watcher mode, including polling |
| `ATLAS_PROFILE` | **Since 0.1.48.** Pin the machine profile tier: `eco`, `balanced`, `performance`, or `turbo`. Unset means auto-detect. See *Machine Profiles* below |
| `ATLAS_MEMORY_LIMIT` | Soft Go heap limit for the Atlas process. Accepts a byte count or a suffixed size (`512MiB`, `2GiB`, `2GB`). Overrides whatever the profile would set |
| `ATLAS_GOGC` | GC target percent. Overrides both the profile default and the warm-daemon nudge |
| `ATLAS_MCP_CALL_TIMEOUT` | Bound an MCP tool call |
